# Quality control analysis

## The Levey-Jennings Chart and Westgard Rules

Levey-Jennings (LJ) charts are widely used in clinical and analytical laboratories as part of their quality control (QC) processes. They provide a visual representation of repeated experimental measurements of a known standard (an analyte of known concentration). These measurements are often taken daily (or every 12 hours in a 24-hour environment). The LJ chart allows the scientist to assess the consistency and reliability of an experimental procedure. Outliers, (or violations) are identified by following a set of rules. NHS pathology services and many analytical laboratories follow the <a href="https://westgard.com/westgard-rules.html" target="_blank">Westgard Rules</a>. These outliers may indicate that the experimental procedure is not performing to the required standard. However, as we shall see below, occasional outliers are expected even under normal conditions, as random variation in data following a normal distribution will produce such values.

Below, we will generate a Levey-Jennings chart and apply a set of rules to identify outliers. We only need the tidyverse for everything that follows.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```

We need to generate some sample data. The "run" is the day of the assay (1–30) and the "value" is the result of the assay.

```{r}
run <- c(1:30)
value <- c(50.0, 49.1, 53.1, 52.9, 50.6, 49.4, 51.3, 52.3, 50.2, 50.1, 49.8, 49.2,  49.2, 51.4, 50.3, 51.2, 51.8, 49.1, 49.2, 49.9, 49.4, 49.0, 49.6, 49.4, 48.2, 49.4, 48.0, 50.4, 51.2, 54.4)
df <- tibble(run = run, value = value)
```

We will now generate a Levey-Jennings plot of the data. The blue line is the mean. The coloured dashed lines show ±1, ±2, and ±3 sigma (σ) from the mean.

Both the mean and sigma are calculated from the data. Sigma is estimated using the **XmR method**: we take the average of the absolute differences between consecutive measurements (the *moving range*) and divide by 1.128. This gives a better estimate of process variability than the overall standard deviation, because it is more sensitive to sudden shifts in the process and less affected by a single large outlier.

First we compute the control limit values, then pass them to ggplot.

```{r}
# Compute control limits
mean_val <- df |> summarise(mean(value)) |> pull()
sigma    <- df |>                                    # XmR sigma estimate:
  mutate(mr = abs(value - lag(value))) |>            # moving range between consecutive points
  summarise(mean(mr, na.rm = TRUE) / 1.128) |>       # average MR divided by d2 constant
  pull()
```

```{r}
df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = run, y = value)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean_val,                        colour = "blue",    linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean_val + c(-1, 1) * sigma,     colour = "orange",  linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean_val + c(-2, 2) * sigma,     colour = "red",     linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean_val + c(-3, 3) * sigma,     colour = "darkred", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point() +
  annotate("text",
           x      = 31,
           y      = mean_val + c(-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3) * sigma,
           label  = c("-3σ", "-2σ", "-1σ", "mean", "+1σ", "+2σ", "+3σ"),
           hjust  = 0, size = 3,
           colour = c("darkred", "red", "orange", "blue", "orange", "red", "darkred")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1, 34)) +
  labs(x = "Run", y = "Value") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Look at the plot above and compare these results to the <a href="https://westgard.com/westgard-rules.html" target="_blank">Westgard Rules</a>.

In the data above, three of the Westgard rules have been violated. Can you identify the runs that are a problem? No code is required here — simply look at the plot above and compare the result to the Westgard Rules on the website above.

Check your answer by running the code below. This generates a facet plot, highlighting violations in red.

The code first defines a small helper function, `flag_run()`, which marks points that belong to a run of **n** or more consecutive `TRUE` values. It uses base R's `rle()` (run-length encoding) to find runs, marks those long enough, and expands the result back to the original length. We then use this function to build a tidy dataset of violations, and plot it separately.

-   **Same Side**: 8 or more consecutive, same-side points (i.e. all above or all below the mean)
-   **1σ**: 4 or more consecutive, same-side points exceeding 1 sigma
-   **2σ**: 2 or more consecutive, same-side points exceeding 2 sigma
-   **3σ**: any points exceeding 3 sigma

```{r}
# flag_run(): marks positions that belong to a run of n or more consecutive TRUEs
# uses base R rle() (run-length encoding) internally
flag_run <- function(condition, n) {
  r <- rle(condition)
  rep(r$lengths >= n & r$values, r$lengths)
}
```

```{r}
# Data prep: classify each point by which rules it violates, then reshape to long format
df_violations <- df |>
  mutate(
    v_same_side = flag_run(value > mean_val, 8) | flag_run(value < mean_val, 8),
    v_1sigma    = flag_run(value > mean_val + sigma,     4) | flag_run(value < mean_val - sigma,     4),
    v_2sigma    = flag_run(value > mean_val + 2 * sigma, 2) | flag_run(value < mean_val - 2 * sigma, 2),
    v_3sigma    = abs(value - mean_val) > 3 * sigma
  ) |>
  select(run, value, starts_with("v_")) |>
  pivot_longer(cols      = starts_with("v_"),
               names_to  = "rule",
               values_to = "violated") |>
  mutate(rule = case_when(
    rule == "v_same_side" ~ "Same Side (8+ consecutive)",
    rule == "v_1sigma"    ~ "1σ (4+ consecutive)",
    rule == "v_2sigma"    ~ "2σ (2+ consecutive)",
    rule == "v_3sigma"    ~ "3σ (any point)"
  ))
```

```{r}
df_violations |>
  ggplot(aes(x = run, y = value)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean_val, colour = "blue", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = violated), size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "black", "TRUE" = "red")) +
  facet_wrap(~ rule) +
  labs(x = "Run", y = "Value") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Notice that the first of these rules is not identical to the Westgard rule. This implementation is slightly more sensitive: it highlights violations where there are 8 or more consecutive same-side points, while the equivalent Westgard rule states 10 or more same-side points. The other three rules have a direct Westgard equivalent.

This is important as various sets of rules for detecting out-of-control or non-random conditions have been proposed and used for different applications:

-   Walter A. Shewhart (1923) Economic Control Of Quality Of Manufactured Product
-   Western Electric Rules — Western Electric Company (1956), Statistical Quality Control Handbook. (1 ed.)
-   Nelson Rules (1984)
-   <a href="https://westgard.com/westgard-rules.html" target="_blank">Westgard Rules</a> (1981)

::: callout-warning
## Important

Always follow the protocol and quality control processes that are used in your workplace – it will vary!
:::

## Testing for outliers using normally distributed data

The data provided above was deliberately manipulated to introduce three rule violations. If this was your actual data from one month in an analytical laboratory, it would indicate that serious errors are occurring on a regular basis. You would need to rectify the problem(s) before running any real samples. If your data is from a normal distribution then outliers detected by these rules are quite rare, but they do happen, even if nothing is wrong with the equipment or the user. Use the code below to generate QC plots of 30 data points from a normal distribution with a mean of 40 and SD = 2. Run this code chunk 12 times (press **Ctrl+Shift+Enter** / **Cmd+Shift+Enter** inside the chunk) to see how often outliers might occur in one year under ideal conditions.<br> Remember, if any outliers are detected, even at these rare intervals, you would still need to check all of your equipment and reagents, as you would have no way of knowing if it is a malfunction or just random noise.

```{r}
# Generate random data — remove set.seed() to get fresh data on every run
set.seed(NULL)

random_df <- tibble(
  run   = 1:30,
  value = rnorm(30, mean = 40, sd = 2)
)
```

```{r}
# Compute control limits for the random data
rand_mean  <- random_df |> summarise(mean(value)) |> pull()
rand_sigma <- random_df |>
  mutate(mr = abs(value - lag(value))) |>
  summarise(mean(mr, na.rm = TRUE) / 1.128) |>
  pull()
```

```{r}
# Data prep: classify violations, reshape to long format
rand_violations <- random_df |>
  mutate(
    v_same_side = flag_run(value > rand_mean, 8) | flag_run(value < rand_mean, 8),
    v_1sigma    = flag_run(value > rand_mean + rand_sigma,     4) | flag_run(value < rand_mean - rand_sigma,     4),
    v_2sigma    = flag_run(value > rand_mean + 2 * rand_sigma, 2) | flag_run(value < rand_mean - 2 * rand_sigma, 2),
    v_3sigma    = abs(value - rand_mean) > 3 * rand_sigma
  ) |>
  select(run, value, starts_with("v_")) |>
  pivot_longer(cols      = starts_with("v_"),
               names_to  = "rule",
               values_to = "violated") |>
  mutate(rule = case_when(
    rule == "v_same_side" ~ "Same Side (8+ consecutive)",
    rule == "v_1sigma"    ~ "1σ (4+ consecutive)",
    rule == "v_2sigma"    ~ "2σ (2+ consecutive)",
    rule == "v_3sigma"    ~ "3σ (any point)"
  ))
```

```{r}
rand_violations |>
  ggplot(aes(x = run, y = value)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = rand_mean, colour = "blue", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = violated), size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "black", "TRUE" = "red")) +
  facet_wrap(~ rule) +
  labs(x = "Run", y = "Value") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: callout-tip
## Question

How many times were outliers detected?<br> Why are these rules designed so that outliers are rare?
:::

## Further Work

You may have noticed that in the first graph above, the mean was 50.3. This value was calculated from the data. In many analytical processes, the standard will be of a known concentration and the process will have a well established standard deviation. Let us assume that for the data above, the known standard should be 50 units with a standard deviation of 1.3. Can you write R-code to generate a plot of the same data but with:

-   with a blue dashed horizontal line at exactly 50 units, label it "50" or "mean"
-   with faint red dashed lines to indicate 1, 2 or 3 standard deviations from 50. Label these lines with "-1 SD", "+1 SD", "-2 SD", "+2 SD" etc.

::: callout-tip
## Tips

use geom_seqment rather than geom_hline as this allows you to control the endpoint with xend = 30

use annotate to add a text label. Set the x = 30.5 as this is the right-side of the plot. Set the y-value to the correct numerical values to get -1 SD, +1 SD, -2 SD, +2 SD etc
:::

```{r}
#this is to get you started
df |> ggplot(aes(x= run, y=value))+ geom_line()+geom_point()+
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = 30, y = 50, yend = 50), # sets the start and end points
               color = "blue",                           # makes it blue
               linetype = "dashed",                     # dashed
               linewidth = 0.5) +                            # fine
  annotate("text", x = 30.5, y = 50, label = "50", hjust = 0, color = "blue") # adds the label "50"
```

-   Western Electric Rules - Western Electric Company (1956), _Statistical Quality Control Handbook_ (1 ed.).
